items.title: AI-Assisted Business Ideation as a Technology–Cognition–Institutional Pathway to Entrepreneurial Intention: A Serial Mediation Model of Perceived Feasibility and Entrepreneurial Consultancy Services
items.abstract: Generative AI has significantly reduced the effort and expense of developing and refining venture ideas, without eliminating the uncertainty and resource limitations of executing a venture. This research examines the potential of AI-assisted business ideation (AIBI) to drive behavioral change in accessing entrepreneurial support infrastructure. The study uses technology-cognition-institutional framework to examine the relationship between AIBI and perceived feasibility (PF) and entrepreneurial consultancy services engagement (ECS) and how these two variables mediate the relationship between AIBI and entrepreneurial intentions (EI). The study analyzed data from 319 university students in Pakistan using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). It evaluated the reliability and validity of the measurement model and examined structural relationships through bootstrapping with bias-corrected confidence intervals. Findings indicate that AI-based business ideation positively affects perceived feasibility, which in turn enhances engagement with entrepreneurial creative strategies (ECS).Moreover, ECS positively and significantly affect entrepreneurial intention, this in turn has a positive and significant direct effect on AIBI. The pathway from AIBI to perceived feasibility to engagement in entrepreneurial consultancy services to entrepreneurial intention is significant, emphasizing that AIBI affects entrepreneurial intention both cognitively and institutionally. This study extends AI entrepreneurship research by showing that AI's effects on entrepreneurial intention go beyond boosting entrepreneurial cognition. This study also contributes to existing intention models by conceptualizing entrepreneurial consultancy services as an endogenous behavioral mediator rather than a contextual condition, offering a more complete explanation of AI-enabled ideation's role in entrepreneurial readiness.

items.title: AI-Based Network Intrusion Detection System Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI
items.abstract: Network intrusion detection is an important cybersecurity function because network traffic can contain benign activity as well as malicious behavior. This paper presents an AI-based Network Intrusion Detection System (AI-NIDS) that combines live packet capture, flow generation, machine-learning classification, explainable artificial intelligence, and web-based visualization. The prototype is implemented in an Ubuntu virtual machine hosted through VirtualBox. Scapy captures traffic visible on the virtual network interface, and related packets are grouped into flows. Four features that can be derived directly from live traffic—destination port, packet count, total bytes, and average packet size—are used by the live classification pipeline. CICIDS2017 is used for model training and evaluation. Isolation Forest is used for anomaly-oriented analysis, while Random Forest and XGBoost perform multi-class classification. SHAP provides feature-level explanations, and a Flask dashboard presents live flows, detections, and explanations. On a held-out test set of 22,339 samples, Random Forest achieved 90.67% accuracy and XGBoost achieved 94.42% accuracy; macro F1 scores were 0.78 and 0.81, respectively. The results demonstrate the feasibility of combining machine learning and explainability in a practical NIDS prototype, while highlighting limitations related to reduced live features, rare attack classes, false positives, and virtualized network scope.

items.title: AI-Driven Credit Scoring and Financial Justice among Young Entrepreneurs in Dhaka City: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: The lack of access to finance is a major issue for young entrepreneurs, especially those who have poor credit scores, lack financial statements and have no collateral. Artificial intelligence (AI) based credit scoring systems have been seen as a potential solution to credit assessment using alternative data, but there are concerns about fairness, transparency, accountability and algorithmic exclusion. This study aims to understand the impact of AI-powered credit scoring on financial justice for young entrepreneurs in Dhaka City, focusing on perceptions of financial access, AI-driven lending opportunities, ethical concerns, and responsible decision-making practices. The study uses a qualitative research approach and thematic analysis to explore the experiences and perspectives of entrepreneurs on traditional credit assessment systems and AI-powered lending mechanisms. The results show that AI-powered credit scoring is seen as a potential means to financial inclusion, as it can include alternative data like digital transaction records and business activity data. But there are also important issues of algorithmic bias, data quality, privacy, transparency, and the risk of leaving out people with small digital footprints, participants note. The study also shows that in the context of AI-driven lending, financial justice encompasses not merely the opportunity to obtain a loan, but also procedural fairness, transparency or explain ability, accountability, and the ability to object to or challenge automated decisions. The study adds to the literature on responsible AI and financial inclusion by offering a socio-technical approach that combines technological innovation and human-centered governance. The results indicate that AI-based credit scoring can contribute to inclusive entrepreneurial finance if applied in an ethically guided, transparent, and accountable manner with proper human supervision.

items.title: AI-Driven Governance in India: Balancing Administrative Efficiency, Transparency, Accountability and Data Protection
items.abstract: India is embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in public administration at the very moment its legal architecture for data protection, transparency and AI oversight is being rewritten. Between November 2025 and August 2026, the government issued the India AI Governance Guidelines, notified the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules 2025, hosted the AI Impact Summit, and began defending in the Supreme Court a constitutional challenge to the DPDP Act's amendment of the Right to Information (RTI) Act. This paper asks whether administrative efficiency, transparency, accountability and data protection can be reconciled in AI-driven governance in India. Using doctrinal analysis, policy analysis and a case study of Telangana's Samagra Vedika welfare-profiling system, it argues that the four values are not inherently opposed. The tensions arise from design choices, thin institutional capacity and broad exemptions for the State. The paper identifies four structural gaps: voluntary AI guidance without enforceable duties; consent-free State processing and wide exemptions under the DPDP Act; the narrowing of the RTI public-interest test; and the absence of a right to human review and explanation. It proposes a proportionality-based, risk-tiered framework combining statutory authorisation, impact assessments, algorithm registers, meaningful human review, independent audit and accessible redress. Legal positions are stated as at 28 September 2026.

items.abstract: Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs), commonly known as submarine drones, provide a critical capability for modern naval operations requiring persistent presence in contested and GPS denied environments. This paper addresses autonomous positioning and area keeping of AUVs within predefined underwater zones using integrated inertial, acoustic, and velocity based navigation systems. Artificial intelligence techniques, including machine learning–based sensor fusion and adaptive decision making, enhance state estimation, navigation robustness, and control performance in uncertain and dynamic environments. By combining AI enabled perception with robust control algorithms, AUVs can maintain precise station keeping and boundary awareness while compensating for ocean currents and environmental disturbances. These capabilities support force protection, intelligence gathering, and undersea surveillance missions, enabling discreet and sustained operations with minimal human intervention.

items.title: AI-ENABLED BLOCKCHAIN ARCHITECTURE FOR TRUSTED IoT DATA MANAGEMENT ACROSS THE CHEMICAL LIFECYCLE: A REFERENCE FRAMEWORK FOR SAUDI ARABIA'S CHEMICAL INDUSTRY
items.abstract: Chemical manufacturers and distributors are increasingly dependent upon a steady stream of data from sensors, lab systems, logistics platforms and connected assets. However, when records are fragmented, unverifiable, or difficult to exchange across organisational boundaries, lifecycle decisions remain exposed to avoidable uncertainty. This review examines the integration of artificial intelligence, blockchain, and the Industrial Internet of Things within a trusted data architecture for the chemical lifecycle in Saudi Arabia. A structured integrative review synthesised peer-reviewed studies mainly published between 2020 and 2025 on industrial IoT security, edge intelligence, blockchain provenance, federated learning, digital twins, smart-contract governance, and supply chain traceability. The evidence indicates that no single technology resolves the trust problem in isolation. Artificial intelligence can spot anomalous or implausible process data, but its outputs inherit the weaknesses of the data pipeline. Blockchain can preserve event provenance and enforce multi-party rules, but high-frequency telemetry should not be directly stored on-chain. The IoT offers operational visibility but the attack surface is expanded by heterogeneous devices, legacy protocols, and weak identities. The review therefore develops a layered architecture where raw telemetry resides in governed off-chain stores, critical lifecycle events are hashed and signed to a permissioned consortium ledger, and edge or federated intelligence provides validation, anomaly detection, predictive functions, and decision support. The proposed design offers auditable event commitments that tie feedstock receipt, processing, quality release, storage, transport, downstream handoff and recovery. For organisations operating in Saudi Arabia's chemical industry, identity governance, semantic interoperability, latency-aware partitioning, privacy-preserving analytics, accountable smart contracts, and phased integration with existing operational technology are central implementation priorities. The review concludes that trusted lifecycle management is less about maximising blockchain usage and more about allocating a narrow, verifiable role for each technology within an end-to-end governance model.

items.title: AI-Enabled Interoperability in Intelligent Digital Systems: A Socio-Technical Framework for Secure, Scalable, and Privacy-Preserving Integration
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), biometric recognition, intelligent transportation systems, distributed energy platforms, and connected vehicles has resulted in increasingly heterogeneous digital infrastructures. Although these systems generate substantial quantities of data and provide sophisticated analytical capabilities, their effectiveness is frequently constrained by fragmented architectures, incompatible data representations, isolated databases, security vulnerabilities, and inadequate mechanisms for trusted information exchange. Interoperability has therefore emerged as a fundamental requirement for the development of intelligent digital ecosystems. However, interoperability cannot be treated exclusively as a technical problem because data integration also involves organizational, semantic, institutional, privacy, security, and governance considerations. This paper investigates the relationship between AI and interoperability and develops a conceptual socio-technical framework for integrating heterogeneous intelligent systems. The study synthesizes research concerning machine-learning-based face recognition, electronic toll collection, peer-to-peer energy trading, human-bot discrimination, federated intrusion detection, low-code/no-code intelligent automation, and secure computing. Particular attention is given to data classification, standardization, semantic compatibility, data friction, privacy-preserving computation, and secure AI deployment. The analysis demonstrates that AI can improve interoperability through intelligent classification, entity matching, anomaly detection, prediction, and automated decision support. Conversely, interoperable infrastructures can improve AI by providing access to more diverse and contextually relevant information. Nevertheless, increasing interoperability can also amplify privacy risks, surveillance capabilities, security threats, algorithmic bias, and unauthorized secondary use of data. The proposed framework consequently combines data and semantic interoperability with AI services, security controls, privacy-preserving mechanisms, governance, and continuous evaluation. The paper concludes that successful AI-enabled interoperability requires a balanced approach in which technical integration is accompanied by standardized representations, privacy-by-design, decentralized learning where appropriate, secure interfaces, transparent governance, and continuous performance assessment.

items.title: AI-enabled nystagmus analysis in vestibular assessment: Current evidence and future directions
items.abstract: Vestibular disorders are common, heterogeneous, and diagnostically challenging. Nystagmus is an important sign in vestibular assessment, but its interpretation can depend on clinician expertise and recording quality. This structured narrative review mapped current evidence on artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled nystagmus and eye-movement signal analysis in vestibular assessment, focusing on study characteristics, input data, AI tasks, model architectures, validation approaches, performance metrics, explainability, and clinical applicability. A structured PubMed search identified human studies that developed, validated, or evaluated machine-learning, deep-learning, or related computational methods for nystagmus analysis or vestibular diagnostic support. Fifteen studies were included, most published from 2021 onwards. The evidence was dominated by technical and early-stage model-development studies using VNG/VOG recordings, other eye-movement recordings, or derived features such as pupil trajectories, optical-flow maps, eye and head traces, and slow-phase velocity measures. Applications included nystagmus detection, pupil tracking and signal extraction, pattern or direction classification, quantification or localisation, and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo-related diagnostic classification. Deep-learning approaches, particularly convolutional neural networks and CNN-recurrent hybrid models, were commonly used. However, validation was mainly internal, performance reporting was heterogeneous, explainability was limited, and prospective workflow evaluation or routine clinical implementation was uncommon. AI-enabled nystagmus analysis shows promising clinical potential, particularly for VNG/VOG-based assessment and BPPV-related decision support. Translation into routine practice will require multicentre patient-level external validation, transparent reporting, interpretable outputs, standardised performance metrics, and prospective evaluation in real clinical pathways.

items.title: AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.

items.title: AI-Mediated Organizational Communication and Crisis Management: Trust, Transparency, and Stakeholder Perception
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming embedded in organisational communication through message generation, conversational agents, monitoring systems, decision support, and automated service recovery. During crises, these functions offer speed, scale, consistency, and continuous availability, but they also change how stakeholders infer agency, competence, care, responsibility, and authenticity. This critical narrative review integrates crisis communication, organisational trust, human–automation trust, artificial intelligence-mediated communication, public relations, and service-recovery research to examine when AI-mediated communication is likely to sustain or erode stakeholder trust. The evidence indicates that no uniform ‘AI effect’ exists. Stakeholder responses depend on whether AI assists a human communicator or appears to replace one, whether the task is informational or relational, whether the crisis demands empathy and moral accountability, whether AI involvement is disclosed, and whether human responsibility remains visible. Technical or process transparency can strengthen perceived accountability and system trust, while simple disclosure that a message was produced with AI may reduce perceived legitimacy, authenticity, or credibility in some contexts. Anthropomorphic cues can increase social presence and perceived empathy, yet they may also raise expectations that become costly when the system fails. Evidence from crisis-response experiments, organisational studies, chatbot research, and service recovery therefore favours calibrated human–AI orchestration over indiscriminate automation. The review proposes that trustworthy AI-mediated crisis communication requires fit among task, crisis responsibility, stakeholder vulnerability, disclosure purpose, system reliability, and accountable human oversight. Current confidence is constrained by a literature dominated by short-term experiments, consumer and convenience samples, hypothetical crises, and limited longitudinal or field evidence. Research should move towards preregistered factorial studies, live crisis simulations, cross-cultural and multi-stakeholder designs, longitudinal trust measurement, and explicit testing of governance and escalation arrangements.

items.title: AI-Powered Adaptive Learning and Smart Education Platform
items.abstract: Education is becoming increasingly digital, yet many students still face difficulties in understanding complex concepts, remembering long answers, identifying their learning gaps, and preparing effectively for examinations. This paper presents an AI-powered adaptive learning platform designed to provide personalized and interactive learning support. The system uses Artificial Intelligence to explain questions in detail, generate short exam-oriented answers and recall keywords, analyze students' performance, identify knowledge gaps, and recommend suitable learning tasks. The platform also provides 3D visualization for mathematical and geometric concepts, AI-assisted learning for languages such as Marathi and Sanskrit with Hindi and English explanations, AI-based viva examination, instant tests, PDF/notes-based learning, progress tracking, and gamification. The main aim is to make learning personalized, understandable, interactive, and focused on actual student improvement rather than simply providing answers

items.title: AI-Powered Automated Assignment Generation and Intelligent Evaluation System Using Natural Language Processing and OpenAI API for Enhanced Learning and Fair Assessment
items.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has precipitated a dual crisis: the exponential increase in faculty workload regarding assessment scalability and the destabilization of traditional academic integrity verification methods. This paper introduces the proposed system, an automated academic evaluation platform designed to address these challenges through a unified, immutable assessment pipeline. Unlike traditional Learning Management Systems (LMS) that function primarily as repositories, the proposed system employs Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate the entire grading lifecycle, from submission to feedback generation, while simultaneously performing rigorous authorship verification. The system enforces a single-submission policy to streamline administrative workflows and generates immutable, audit-ready reports containing scoring rationale and AIgenerated content likelihood. The system architecture, scoring methodology, and a multi-layered integrity detection approach based on stylometry and machine learning classifiers are described. Simulated performance results suggest that the proposed system mitigates the subjective variability of human grading while offering a scalable solution to the integrity challenges posed by unrestricted GenAI access.

items.title: AI-Supported Blockchain Technology for Reducing Non-Revenue Water: A Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: Non-revenue water (NRW) — water produced and entering a distribution network but lost before it generates revenue — remains one of the most persistent inefficiencies in urban water management, with global losses estimated at roughly 126 billion cubic meters and USD 39 billion annually. Two technological families have been proposed, largely separately, to address this problem. Artificial intelligence (AI), through machine-learning and deep-learning models applied to pressure, flow, and acoustic data, improves the detection, localization, and prediction of leaks. Blockchain, a form of distributed ledger technology, offers a complementary capability: securing metering data, automating billing through smart contracts, and making reported consumption and loss figures auditable across multiple institutional stakeholders. This chapter argues that these two technologies address different parts of the same problem — AI improves analytical capability, while blockchain improves the trustworthiness of the data analyzed — and that treating them as substitutes rather than complements understates their combined potential. Building on this premise, the chapter develops a conceptual, three-layer architecture integrating an IoT-based data-acquisition layer, an AI analytics layer for leak detection and predictive maintenance, and a blockchain layer for data integrity and institutional trust, with a digital twin emerging as an integration concept rather than a separate technological layer. The framework is illustrated with reference to Türkiye’s regulatory context and to Gaziantep Su ve Kanalizasyon İdaresi (GASKİ), a metropolitan water and sewerage administration that reduced its reported NRW rate from above 49 percent in 2014 to approximately 25 percent in 2025, a trajectory its own management attributes partly to AI-integrated SCADA systems and precision pressure management. The chapter reviews pilot-level and early operational evidence for both technologies, distinguishes peer-reviewed findings from preprint and vendor material, and acknowledges that empirical support remains considerably stronger for AI-based leak management than for blockchain integration at utility scale. It concludes that public utilities facing legal and financial accountability for reported performance should prioritize reliable metering and AI-based analytics first, while testing blockchain in a single, high-value governance use case such as contractor-performance verification, and proposes a research agenda comparing otherwise similar systems with and without blockchain-based integrity assurance.

items.title: AI-Supported Management Accounting and Decision-Making Processes: A Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: Advances in digital transformation, Industry 4.0, and big data technologies are fundamentally changing the competitive landscape in which businesses operate and reshaping traditional decision-making processes. Artificial intelligence, which lies at the heart of this technological transformation, not only automates business processes but also elevates them to a strategic level through its high data processing speed, continuous learning capabilities, and advanced predictive capabilities. Management accounting, which lies at the heart of businesses’ financial and strategic data flows, is significantly affected by this transformation. Artificial intelligence technologies are helping management accounting evolve beyond its traditional functions of data collection, processing, and reporting toward a more analytical and predictive framework. This transformation is opening up new possibilities in various management accounting practices, such as cost management, performance evaluation, financial forecasting, and the analysis of resource utilization. In particular, artificial intelligence’s advanced analytical capabilities enable managers to assess the company’s current situation more comprehensively and respond more quickly to changing conditions. Thus, the role of management accounting within the organization is evolving into a more active structure that goes beyond the presentation of financial information regarding past periods to generate forward-looking information and support strategic decision-making processes. The purpose of this study is to examine the impact of artificial intelligence technologies on management accounting and decision-making processes. The integration of artificial intelligence technologies into management accounting is driving transformation in various application areas, such as cost management, performance evaluation, and financial forecasting. To make effective use of artificial intelligence technologies, it is necessary to take into account factors such as data quality, data security and privacy, technological infrastructure, ethical principles, organizational conditions, and employees’ digital competencies. In addition, it is evident that artificial intelligence has not completely replaced human expertise in management accounting; human expertise remains important, particularly in activities that require professional judgment, interpretation, and strategic decision-making. For this reason, artificial intelligence is viewed not as a technology that replaces management accountants, but as a complementary tool that supports their analytical and strategic roles. In conclusion, the integration of artificial intelligence into management accounting can help businesses use data more effectively, support decision-making processes, and strengthen the strategic role of management accounting. In future research, it will be important to determine how management accounting tasks can be shared between humans and artificial intelligence, and in which tasks professional expertise and judgment will remain essential.

items.title: Algorithmic justice in the making: AI, sentencing, and fairness in Malaysia’s criminal courts
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in criminal justice systems to improve efficiency and consistency, but its use in sentencing raises important questions about fairness, transparency, and judicial discretion. This article examines Malaysia’s introduction of AI-assisted sentencing through the Artificial Intelligence in Court Sentencing (AiCOS) system and asks how algorithmic assistance reshapes the exercise and visibility of sentencing discretion. It adopts a qualitative, desk-based, and interdisciplinary approach, drawing on criminology, legal and sociolegal scholarship, judicial and institutional materials, and international AI governance frameworks. The Malaysian experience is examined through four dimensions: transparency and explainability, procedural contestability, human discretion, and accountability, with comparative reference to the United States’s experience with COMPAS (Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions) and the European Union’s regulatory framework. The article argues that AiCOS is best understood not as an autonomous ‘AI judge’, but as an automated evolution of Malaysia’s existing Table of Sentencing . While its guidance function remains broadly similar, algorithmic mediation changes the visibility and contestability of the basis upon which punishment is determined. Automation therefore does not eliminate discretion but may relocate it into less visible decisions concerning data, system design, deployment, and reliance on algorithmic recommendations. The article concludes that retaining a human judge as the final decision-maker is insufficient, by itself, to ensure fairness. Effective governance requires transparency, disclosure, meaningful opportunities to challenge algorithmic inputs and recommendations, reasoned judicial decision-making, and continuing independent oversight.

items.title: ALGORITHMIC PERSONALIZATION AND CONSUMER TRUST IN EMERGING DIGITAL MARKETS: A CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK FOR MARKETING MANAGEMENT IN UZBEKISTAN
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a central instrument of contemporary marketing, particularly in the form of algorithmic personalization of offers, messages and recommendations. While the literature in advanced economies documents both the commercial value of personalization and the consumer resistance it can provoke, emerging digital markets remain comparatively underexplored. This conceptual paper develops an integrative framework that explains how the quality of AI-driven personalization translates into purchase intention and loyalty in an emerging-market setting, using Uzbekistan as the reference context. Drawing on research on AI in marketing, algorithm aversion, organizational trust and information privacy, the paper positions consumer trust in the AI system as the key mediating mechanism and identifies algorithmic transparency and perceived human oversight as its principal antecedents. Perceived privacy risk and decision involvement are proposed as boundary conditions, and linguistic and cultural fit is introduced as a context-specific component of personalization quality. Five testable propositions are formulated, a four-phase research design is outlined, and managerial implications are presented for firms operating in mobile-first, multilingual markets with fast-growing e-commerce and fintech sectors. The paper concludes with a research agenda for empirical validation.

items.title: An Explainable Deep Learning Model for Breast Cancer Subtype Prediction Using Gene Expression Data
items.abstract: The sub-typing of breast cancer plays a vital role in personalizing oncology by guiding treatment strategies and prognosis. This study proposes a new approach by integrating deep learning and large language models (LLMs) for subtype prediction based on gene expression. The approach includes unsupervised clustering using K-Means so as to identify the hidden expression patterns, followed by a Multi-layer Perceptron Feedforward Neural Network for supervised classification of BRCA subtypes. In order to improve the interpretability, Llama 3.1 model was fine-tuned on prompt response pairs that were derived from gene subtype associations, generating textual explanations for the predicted class. The model gave promising results, with 91 percent accuracy, thus demonstrating strong potential for clinical insight generation. Additionally, the model is tested with dataset of lung cancer, confirming its generalizability among tumour types.

items.title: An Improved Retrieval-Augmented Generation Agent for UAV Situation Awareness Report Generation
items.abstract: Accurate and timely UAV (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) situation awareness is essential for early warning and operational decision-making in low-altitude security, yet the manual analysis of large-scale heterogeneous data is resource-intensive and introduces delays. This study proposes IRAG-UAVSA (Improved Retrieval-Augmented Generation—Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Situation Awareness) Agent, an autonomous situation-awareness report-generation framework based on an improved retrieval-augmented generation architecture. The framework integrates real-time UAV descriptors, including platform type, intent, and threat level, with four task-specific hierarchical knowledge bases. A dual-loop pipeline combines evidence-template-guided hybrid retrieval and cross-encoder reranking with high-level LLM (Large Language Model) reflection, structured evidence filling, rule-based validation, and threshold-triggered iterative retry. A three-level evaluation framework was designed, comprising process-level RAG metrics, automatic natural language evaluation, and human–LLM collaborative scoring. Across 49 domain-screened test inputs, IRAG-UAVSA Agent achieved 93.0% knowledge coverage, 4.1% hallucination, and 91.7% logical consistency, while also obtaining the best SummaC (0.67) and VeriScore (0.83) results among the evaluated baselines. The results indicate that iterative retrieval with explicit evidence constraints can substantially improve the factual grounding, traceability, and practical utility of LLM-generated UAV situation-awareness reports.

items.title: An Intelligent Integration Layer for Physics–AI Collaboration in Digital Drilling: Architecture, Interface Contracts, and Numerical Demonstration
items.abstract: Drilling systems generate abundant predictions from sensors, physics-based models, digital twins, and artificial intelligence (AI), yet the step from prediction to engineering decision remains fragmented across modules and human expertise, and no established framework specifies how uncertain, heterogeneous predictions should be combined and checked against hard limits before an action is taken. This research article proposes, specifies, and numerically demonstrates an Intelligent Integration Layer (IIL) between model outputs and control execution. The gap is diagnosed as three interface defects: heterogeneous uncertainty that is not fused, uncertainty truncated to point estimates at module boundaries, and hard limits that are softened into penalties or checked only against nominal predictions. The IIL addresses these through three stages (Engineering Understanding, Reasoning, and Decision), explicit interface contracts, and a reproducible reasoning procedure in which candidate actions are generated around the current operating point, eliminated by a joint chance constraint, ranked, and assigned a confidence score that gates decision authority. In a synthetic drilling-ahead study, the strongest supported result is that a sample-based joint chance constraint reduced realized constraint violations from 24.6% of reasoning cycles under hard constraints on mean predictions to 1.4%. Confidence gating reduced them further, to 0.7%, but did so largely by referring 65% of cycles to a conservative simulated engineer, and its confidence score did not distinguish reliable from unreliable admissible recommendations; the gated policies are therefore reported as exploratory counterfactuals, and a policy that implements the confidence-authority rule in this reduced simulation, with engineer confirmation as the highest authority, is reported alongside them. The principal contributions are a diagnosis of the prediction-to-decision gap as a set of interface defects rather than model deficiencies; a specification of the integration layer, comprising interface contracts, a reproducible reasoning procedure, and gated levels of decision authority, whose contracts make the dimensions and time dependence of engineering feasibility explicit; and a positioning of that layer relative to chance-constrained optimization, model predictive control, safety filters, and deployed intelligent drilling systems, which clarifies what the IIL adds and what it inherits.

items.title: Anthropometric–Furniture Mismatch among Engineering Students and Preliminary Ergonomic Design Specifications for Engineering Drawing Workstations at Igbinedion University, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study assessed anthropometric characteristics and dimensional compatibility between engineering students and existing engineering-drawing furniture at Igbinedion University, Okada, Nigeria. The analysis used 120 anthropometric records, six chair variants, and one drawing-table configuration. The participant-level work-surface requirement was calculated as popliteal height plus a 2 cm footwear allowance plus sitting elbow height. Popliteal height ranged from 35.9 to 51.7 cm (mean 44.15, SD 2.71); the calculated work-surface requirement had a P5–P95 envelope of 66.40–79.12 cm. Under the stated criteria, seat-height compatibility ranged from 28.33% to 53.33%, seat-depth compatibility from 68.33% to 92.50%, and seat-width compatibility from 82.50% to 93.33% across the six chairs. The 81 cm table had 0% compatibility under the fixed-seat chair–table criterion, while measured knee and thigh clearances accommodated all 120 records. Preliminary anthropometric targets are approximately 41.99–50.21 cm adjustable seat height, 30.85–47.41 cm seat-depth envelope, minimum seat width of 43.41 cm before justified allowances, work-surface height of 66.40–79.12 cm, knee clearance of at least 55.91 cm, and thigh clearance of at least 24.41 cm. The dataset does not contain seated shoulder height, so a backrest-height target could not be derived. These are preliminary targets, not validated specifications; prototype and user testing are required.

items.title: Application of Large Language Models for Design and Monitoring Geotechnical Infrastructure in the Crosshairs of Climate Change Induced Extreme Weather Events
items.abstract: Over the last two decades, climate change events have significantly affected the stability of geotechnical infrastructure, caused damage and resulting in injuries and loss of life. Climate-change events such as heavy rainfall, high temperatures, and permafrost thaw can affect the stability of slopes and embankments, causing problems with tunnel linings and foundation failures. The effects of climate change-induced extreme weather events on geotechnical infrastructure and people's lives can be minimized by using advanced data analysis techniques for monitoring and design. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have become popular for efficient and accurate infrastructure design and monitoring because they are trained on large volumes of data. This review summarizes the contributions of different researchers on the effects of climate change-induced extreme weather events on geotechnical infrastructure, including slopes, tunnels, embankments, and foundations. Moreover, this research proposes avenues for using LLMs for efficient monitoring and design of geotechnical infrastructure. By summarizing the findings, this paper highlights the impact of extreme weather events on geotechnical infrastructure and helps engineers adopt LLMs for the design and monitoring of geotechnical infrastructure. Overall, integrating LLMs into the design and monitoring of geotechnical infrastructure can improve safety by enhancing early-warning systems for slopes, embankments, and tunnels and by enabling designs that account for the variability of environmental forces during extreme weather events.

items.title: Application of large language models in early screening of Alzheimer’s disease: a scoping review
items.abstract: Objective To systematically map the current applications of large language models (LLMs) in the early screening of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and to provide evidence to inform future research and nursing practice. Methods This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodological framework. A comprehensive search was performed in PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, ProQuest, and Scopus from database inception to April 20, 2026. Eligible studies were screened, selected, and synthesized according to predefined inclusion criteria. Results A total of 25 studies were included. The LLMs applied in these studies mainly consisted of general-purpose generative models, multimodal models, and medical-specific models. Data sources primarily included public databases, along with real-world clinical data and simulated data. LLMs were mainly applied for cognitive impairment identification, data augmentation, automated cognitive assessment, and clinical decision support, with cognitive impairment identification being the predominant application direction. Several studies employed prompting strategies including zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought prompting, and agent-based prompting. Multimodal integration and agent-based collaborative reasoning have emerged as important research directions in recent years. Conclusion Large language models provide a novel technological approach for early AD screening and demonstrate potential for supporting cognitive assessment and risk identification. Future research should strengthen real-world studies, multicenter validation, and the development of model safety and ethical governance frameworks to facilitate the standardized application of LLMs in early AD screening.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Administrative Effectiveness Among Pentecostal Churches in South-East Nigeria
items.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and administrative effectiveness among Pentecostal churches in South-East Nigeria. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was adopted, with 240 respondents drawn from Pentecostal churches across Abia, Imo, Enugu, Anambra and Ebonyi States. Respondents comprised senior pastors, administrative secretaries, media/ICT personnel, finance/account personnel, and pastors/heads of departments. The study assessed AI awareness, AI adoption, administrative automation, financial management, communication, decision-making, administrative effectiveness, challenges to adoption and general perceptions of AI. The supplied dataset classified 80 respondents (33.3%) each as low, moderate and high AI adopters. Higher adoption was consistently associated with greater use of AI in administrative automation, financial management, communication and data-supported decision-making, as well as higher administrative-effectiveness scores. Major challenges included skill gaps, cost, internet/connectivity limitations, resistance to change and data-privacy concerns. The study concludes that AI adoption is strongly associated with administrative effectiveness, while emphasizing that the cross-sectional design does not establish causation. Responsible adoption requires AI literacy, adequate infrastructure, data governance, human oversight and clear organizational policies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Buyer–Supplier Relationships in Procurement
items.abstract: This study investigates the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications on buyer–supplier relationship quality in Nigeria's mobile manufacturing sector, with specific reference to TECNO Mobile Nigeria. Drawing on the Commitment-Trust Theory of Relationship Marketing (Morgan & Hunt, 1994), the study operationalises AI through three proxies: Predictive Analytics (PA), Automation of Processes (AP), and AI Risk Management (AIR). A survey research design was adopted, and structured questionnaires were administered to 250 employees and supply chain partners purposively selected from TECNO Mobile's procurement, logistics, IT, and supplier management functions. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics (frequencies, means, standard deviations) and one-sample t-tests benchmarked against the scale's neutral midpoint (μ₀ = 3.00). All three null hypotheses were rejected at p < 0.001. Predictive Analytics recorded an aggregate mean of 3.88 (SD = 0.34; t(249) = 40.53), Automation of Processes 3.91 (SD = 0.36; t(249) = 40.05), and AI Risk Management 3.92 (SD = 0.36; t(249) = 40.47), all significantly above the neutral midpoint. Findings confirm that respondents perceive each AI dimension as positively and meaningfully contributing to trust, efficiency, transparency, and long-term relational stability with suppliers. items.title: Artificial intelligence and digital technologies in railway systems: a systematic literature review using the TCCM framework
items.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed industries worldwide, driving digital innovation operational efficiency, safety, reliability and overall sustainability. Additionally, associated technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, digital twins and the Internet of Things (IoT) have further accelerated the digital transformation across railway systems. The literature in this domain is still at a developmental stage and remains fragmented across multiple application domains. This limits the understanding of theoretical foundations, context and methodological approaches. Design/methodology/approach To address this gap, this study conducts a hybrid systematic literature review using thematic analysis of bibliometric data from 121 Scopus records followed by application of the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM) framework on a subset of the literature identified through systematic screening based on Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Findings The theoretical and conceptual development in this domain is strongly focused on the themes relating to predictive maintenance, infrastructure monitoring and operational optimisation. Novel technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, digital twins and the IoT emerge as the most frequently discussed technologies in the context of adoption within existing systems. The integrated TCCM analysis identifies three broad trajectories: a technology-integration trajectory centred on digital twins, cyber-physical systems and Industry 4.0/5.0; an algorithmic trajectory centred on AI, machine learning, deep learning and prognostics; and a decision-optimisation trajectory involving multi-criteria decision-making, fuzzy logic and intelligent transport systems. There is a comparatively higher concentration of literature on developed economies. Freight and logistics, despite emerging as an important thematic area, remain theoretically and methodologically fragmented, while emerging economies and several passenger- and sustainability-oriented applications receive limited attention. Methodologically, the literature is dominated by reviews, conceptual frameworks, modelling, simulation and experimental studies, with limited longitudinal evidence on the organisational and strategic consequences of AI adoption. There remains scope for stronger theoretical grounding, focusing on freight logistics, emerging technologies and longitudinal investigations to advance the literature. Originality/value This study provides a structured synthesis of the fragmented literature on AI and digital technologies in railway systems through the TCCM framework. It identifies key research gaps and proposes a future research agenda emphasising stronger theoretical foundations, freight-oriented applications, emerging technologies and longitudinal empirical investigations to support the development of intelligent and sustainable railway ecosystems.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Industrial Wastewater Treatment: Bibliometric Trends, Application Areas, and Critical Gaps (2016–2025)
items.abstract: The growing complexity and variability of industrial wastewater (IWW) require treatment strategies that can support reliable prediction, monitoring, optimization, and operational decision-making. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have increasingly been applied to these functions; however, the literature remains fragmented across pollutants, treatment processes, and modeling approaches. This study presents a critical bibliometric review of 151 Scopus-indexed publications on AI/ML applications in IWW treatment published between 2016 and 2025. Publication output increased substantially, reaching 35 publications in 2024 and 67 in 2025, compared with 1–4 publications annually during 2016–2019. China was the leading contributor with 54 publications, followed by India with 26, while Saudi Arabia and the United States each contributed 15. The main research directions included prediction and soft sensing, process optimization and control, monitoring and digitalization, adsorption and material-based treatment, membrane processes, and advanced oxidation and degradation. Artificial neural networks, support vector machines, random forests, and hybrid models were among the most frequently applied techniques. Study-level assessment of 38 technically assessable original AI/ML applications showed that 34 studies (89.5%) relied on offline or retrospective model evaluation, whereas only four (10.5%) demonstrated online or real-time AI/ML evaluation or operation. Conventional internal validation predominated among studies for which validation design could be established, while independent temporal, cross-domain, cross-scale, or field-based validation remained comparatively uncommon. Laboratory- and bench-scale applications were common, although several studies used full-scale industrial data. Major barriers to practical deployment include limited transferability across wastewater matrices, insufficient field-scale validation, inconsistent sensor and data quality, limited interpretability, and weak integration with treatment-plant control systems. Chemical oxygen demand soft sensing, pH and chemical-dosing support, and real-time monitoring and anomaly detection represent promising pathways for near-term implementation, while closed-loop control requires stronger validation of reliability, safety, and long-term performance. Overall, the field is transitioning from isolated, model-centered research toward system-level deployment, where transferability, validation, interpretability, and control integration are as important.

items.title: Artificial intelligence at the surgeon–pathologist interface: revolutionizing diagnosis, prognostication, and precision surgery
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence applications in surgical pathology encompass tumour detection, histological classification, grading, biomarker assessment, lymph node evaluation, margin analysis, and outcome prediction. Deep learning algorithms have demonstrated high diagnostic performance across multiple malignancies including breast, colorectal, prostate, lung, and gastrointestinal cancers. Emerging computational pathology platforms can predict molecular alterations directly from routine haematoxylin and eosin-stained slides, facilitating personalized treatment strategies while reducing dependence on expensive ancillary testing. AI-assisted pathology has also improved workflow efficiency, reduced interobserver variability, and enhanced diagnostic reproducibility. Importantly, AI-derived pathological insights are increasingly influencing surgical decision-making through improved risk stratification, optimized extent of resection, tailored lymphadenectomy, and prediction of treatment response.

items.title: Artificial intelligence at work: Balancing opportunity and fear in shaping employee well-being in the IT sector
items.abstract: BackgroundThis study investigates the complex relationship between perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) opportunities and well-being, exploring the underlying psychological processes. Using conservation of resources theory, we examine how employees who view AI as an opportunity report better workplace well-being and show greater adaptive thinking capacity. Conversely, perceptions of unemployment risk appear to be linked to challenges in cognitive reappraisal, which, in turn, correlate with diminished well-being.ObjectiveTo assess the relationships among these constructs, including the specific relationship between employment insecurity and well-being, to understand how AI is experienced as both a valuable tool and a source of stress.MethodsThis research, conducted among 201 professionals in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, uses convenience sampling and structural equation modeling (analyzed using SPSS and SmartPLS) to assess relationships among these constructs, including the relationship between employment insecurity and well-being.ResultsThe findings suggest that optimism and hope about AI may support psychological resilience, whereas concerns about displacement are negatively correlated with employee well-being.ConclusionUltimately, while grounded in a specific context, this study offers wider implications, showing how AI is experienced as both a valuable tool and a source of stress, depending largely on an individual's assessment of the related risks in their professional environment.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for full-cycle clinical management in orthokeratology: a comprehensive review
items.abstract: The global myopia epidemic, especially among children, poses a major public health burden. Orthokeratology (OK) is an established intervention for slowing myopia progression, yet its conventional practice is constrained by variable treatment responses, an experience-dependent fitting process, and the need for vigilant long-term safety monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers an approach to enhance precision, efficiency, and accessibility across the entire OK care cycle. This review assesses AI applications in OK, encompassing pre-treatment efficacy prediction, AI-assisted lens fitting and automated fit assessment during treatment, and post-treatment safety monitoring with complication risk alert. Evidence indicates that AI models perform comparably to, and in some tasks surpass, human experts in predicting outcomes and determining optimal lens parameters. However, translation from research to routine practice is hindered by limited data quality and diversity, the opacity of complex algorithms, insufficient external validation, and unresolved ethical concerns. Progress depends on building large-scale, diverse datasets, developing interpretable and robust models, and fostering effective human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Imbalanced Financial Classification and Its Societal Implications for Digital Trust: A Cost-Sensitive XGBoost–Transformer Ensemble
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates how financial institutions decide who is trusted, who is scrutinised, and who is refused — decisions that carry direct social consequences for individuals and communities. Automated credit-risk and fraud-assessment systems are deployed at a scale where their errors are not merely statistical but socially consequential, because they can restrict access to credit, widen financial exclusion, and erode public confidence in digital finance. This paper addresses one technical precondition for trustworthy deployment: reliable learning from severely imbalanced financial data. It treats the task as what the data actually measure — prediction of credit-card default rather than verified fraud — and proposes FraudShield, a hybrid framework that combines a gradient-boosting model (XGBoost), a Transformer-based tabular model, an adaptive gating mechanism that learns a per-instance weighting of the two branches, and a cost-sensitive decision layer that reflects the unequal social and economic cost of different errors. The framework is evaluated on the UCI Credit Card Default dataset (30,000 clients), whose positive (default) class comprises 22.12% of the observations — a ratio of approximately 1:3.52. The evaluation protocol splits the data before any preprocessing, fits target encoding and standardization within each training fold only, and applies SMOTE to the training folds alone. Under this corrected protocol, FraudShield attains an AUC-ROC of 0.943 and an F1-score of 0.892, and the cost-sensitive layer raises measured cost savings from 16.7% to 28.4% over the majority-class baseline. The paper interprets these results within a broader discussion of AI accountability, fairness, and digital trust, and argues that technically sound imbalanced-learning methods are a necessary — though not sufficient — condition for socially responsible automated decision-making in finance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Scientific Work: Ethics, Responsibility, and Practical Applications
items.abstract: Workshop held at the Leipzig University Library (more info here). Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming scientific research, but how can we use these technologies responsibly? This workshop goes beyond simply presenting AI tools and instead focuses on the ethical, legal, and sustainable aspects of their application. We critically discuss how AI systems can influence scientific integrity, from data quality to potential biases in research results. Central to this are good scientific practice, data protection, copyright, and sustainability: How can researchers trustfully integrate AI tools without compromising reproducibility or ethical standards? We also explore ethical challenges such as transparency, fairness, and the long-term consequences of AI usage. Only after clarifying these core questions we address practical use: Which AI tools are suitable for which research goals? The workshop provides an insight into the opportunities and risks of AI in science, with the goal of equipping participants with a clear understanding of essential safeguards and best practices, as well as a practical, secure workflow to confidently integrate AI tools into their research without compromising scientific integrity, reproducibility, or compliance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Surrogacy: Legal Challenges, Liability, and the Protection of Vulnerable Parties
items.abstract: Despite the promise of better outcomes and efficiency, artificial intelligence in reproductive technology is changing the legal environment for surrogacy and complicating the family law landscape. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to match intended parents with surrogate mothers, conduct medical screenings and assist parents in making decisions. While the development is bringing benefits, the uncertainty created is uncontrolled. This paper examines the legal implications of AI-assisted surrogacy, focusing on issues of liability, contractual validity, and the determination of parental rights. The involvement of algorithmic systems challenges traditional legal principles, particularly in situations where harm may result from automated decisions or inaccurate data. The lack of transparency further complicates the allocation of responsibility among the different actors involved. From a human rights perspective, the use of AI in surrogacy raises concerns regarding the protection of the best interests of the child, as well as the autonomy and dignity of surrogate mothers. The paper highlights the risks of exploitation and unequal power relations, which may be intensified through technological mediation, especially in cross-border contexts. The paper argues that current legal frameworks are not adequately equipped to regulate the intersection between artificial intelligence and surrogacy, emphasizing the need for clearer legal standards and stronger regulatory oversight to ensure the protection of vulnerable parties.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness, Whistleblowing Systems, and Professional Skepticism in Higher-Education Fraud Detection
items.abstract: Background: Digital transformation has increased the complexity of fraud risks in higher education institutions, requiring governance mechanisms, professional judgment, and technological capabilities to operate in combination. Objective: This research investigates the influence of Whistleblowing Systems and Professional Skepticism on Fraud Detection Effectiveness while examining the direct and moderating roles of Artificial Intelligence Readiness. Methods: A quantitative methodology was employed through a cross-sectional survey involving internal auditors, members of Internal Supervisory Units (Satuan Pengawasan Internal [SPI]), and university staff engaged in governance and fraud prevention across Indonesian higher education institutions. The collected data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results: The findings reveal that Whistleblowing Systems, Professional Skepticism, and Artificial Intelligence Readinesseach have a positive and statistically significant effect on Fraud Detection Effectiveness. Artificial Intelligence Readinessalso significantly strengthens the relationship between Whistleblowing Systems and Fraud Detection Effectiveness but does not significantly moderate the relationship between Professional Skepticism and Fraud Detection Effectiveness. Conclusion: These results suggest that artificial intelligence supports fraud detection not by replacing auditors' professional judgment but by strengthening organizational preparedness to integrate intelligent technologies into governance frameworks. Therefore, effective fraud detection in higher education depends on the synergy among organizational governance, human expertise, and Artificial Intelligence Readiness.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-based analysis of digital media engagement and user sentiment using machine learning techniques
items.abstract: Abstract Digital media datasets consist of both text content and platform, campaign, temporal, and engagement data, but precomputed sentiment and engagement data can lead to target leakage and overestimation of model performance. This study introduces the Hybrid Textual Sentiment Engagement Learning Model (HTSELM), a leakage-controlled late-fusion model for sentiment and engagement analysis. The experiments are conducted with the machine-generated Social Media Engagement Dataset, which has 28 raw columns and 12,000 records. Deterministic Affective Proxies are removed prior to training for the primary sentiment task. The text branch is a TF-IDF Linear Support Vector Machine with a weight of 0.70, and the structured branch is a HistGradientBoosting branch with a weight of 0.30, assigned by validation. On the held-out test set, HTSELM achieves an accuracy of 0.9392, macro-precision of 0.9471, macro-recall of 0.9336, macro-F1 of 0.9398, weighted-F1 of 0.9392, Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.9043, Cohen’s kappa of 0.9040, macro ROC-AUC of 0.9923, and macro PR-AUC of 0.9862. The Mean macro-F1 score for Exact 5-fold cross-validation is 0.9398 with an SD of 0.0069. Ablation shows that the dominant signal is text, and the validation-tuned fusion branch offers a relatively small but stable improvement over the text-only branch. There is minimal degradation due to numeric noise, but missing features and text corruption result in gradual degradation. A prospective engagement experiment (excluding engagement-rate components and post-response variables) is similarly close to chance, and the released pre-response variables are not reliable predictors of engagement. The results highlight the importance of leakage auditing, clear feature fusion and careful interpretation when analyzing digital media.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Visual–Inertial Navigation for Autonomous Lunar Surface Mobility: Systems, Datasets, Methods, and Open Challenges
items.abstract: Reliable onboard state estimation plays an important role in autonomous lunar surface mobility, given the lack of conventional global navigation satellite system (GNSS) coverage and the challenges of variable illumination and terrain texture. This review synthesizes model-based, learning-based, and hybrid visual–inertial odometry (VIO) approaches and assesses their relevance to lunar surface operations. The reviewed studies suggest that learned components can improve feature extraction, matching, depth estimation, and measurement confidence in selected datasets and operating conditions. However, representative lunar validation and uncertainty calibration remain limited. Given these limitations, hybrid architectures integrating learned components with explicit model-based estimators offer a comparatively testable design direction. Reduced lunar gravity alone does not render monocular scale unobservable; practical scale–bias performance also depends jointly on motion excitation, inertial quality, visual geometry, calibration, and estimation-window length. Stereo, wheel, crater, and map cues can provide additional metric information but introduce source-specific risks involving calibration, slip, association, and registration. Within the resources surveyed, we found no publicly available flight-derived lunar traverse dataset combining synchronized camera–IMU measurements, independent trajectory ground truth, and onboard timing. Evidence-based priorities include representative lunar validation, uncertainty-aware integration of learned components, consistency monitoring across metric sources, explicit estimator health and fallback mechanisms, and target-hardware resource evaluation.

items.title: Artificial Superintelligence: Must It Be Everywhere? From the Myth of Talos to Infrastructure Dependencies, Operational Authority, and Human Control
items.abstract: Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) raises important questions about the future of artificial intelligence, its potential benefits, and the possibility of losing human control. While many discussions focus on how powerful ASI could become, less attention is given to where it should be used, what authority it should have, and how its dependence on physical infrastructure may create additional risks. Using Talos, the bronze guardian of Greek mythology, as a metaphor for power and physical dependency, this article examines the differences between Artificial Intelligence (AI), Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), and ASI. The study discusses their capabilities, shared infrastructure requirements, and the motivations behind the development of superintelligence. It also distinguishes risks already observed in current AI research from hypothetical scenarios involving future ASI systems. Specific attention is given to energy and critical infrastructure. The article explores the risks that may arise when an intelligent system is granted control over the infrastructure on which its own operation depends. It emphasizes that intelligence, autonomy, and operational authority are different concepts, and that greater intelligence does not necessarily require greater authority. The article proposes a selective, risk-based approach to ASI deployment, supported by limited access permissions, independent safety mechanisms, infrastructure resilience, and meaningful human oversight. Rather than assuming that superintelligence should be integrated into every system, it argues that its use should be determined by actual needs, expected benefits, resource requirements, and the ability to maintain effective human control.

items.title: Asesmen Pembelajaran SD Melalui Artificial Intelligence Berbantuan Zep Quiz Berbasis Adventure Game-Based Learning
items.abstract: Teachers’ limited capacity to develop engaging and adaptive digital assessments, coupled with the underutilization of artificial intelligence (AI), provided the basis for this community service program. The program aimed to improve teachers’ understanding and digital literacy in developing AI-assisted learning assessments using Zep Quiz within an adventure game-based learning approach. It was implemented at SDN 5 Mojolangu with teachers from the elementary school and Islamic elementary school teachers’ working group (KKG) in Lowokwaru District. The program comprised five stages: socialization, training, technology implementation, mentoring and evaluation, and sustainability planning. Its outcomes were evaluated using attendance records, questionnaires measuring understanding, perceived improvement in digital literacy, and program meaningfulness, as well as the products submitted by participants. The program involved 20 teachers, exceeding the initial target of 15 participants. The evaluation results showed a mean understanding score of 3.85 on a four-point scale, categorized as very high; a mean perceived digital literacy improvement score of 3.80, categorized as a substantial improvement; and a mean program meaningfulness score of 4.00, categorized as highly meaningful. All participants successfully developed and submitted 20 Zep Quiz products. These findings indicate that practice-oriented training and mentoring can help teachers integrate pedagogical considerations with technological skills in assessment development. Program sustainability will be supported through classroom trials, peer reviews within the KKG forum, and periodic evaluations to promote the independent and continuous use of digital assessment.

items.title: Augmenting colonoscopy with artificial intelligence and robotic assistance: a human-factors scoping review toward a task-based shared autonomy paradigm
items.abstract: Colonoscopy is central to colorectal cancer prevention but remains a high-demand psychomotor and cognitive procedure, characterized by operator dependency, variable performance, and substantial physical and mental workload. Increasing evidence links procedural quality and safety to clinician-related factors, including musculoskeletal strain, fatigue, and non-technical skills. Concurrently, artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic technologies are emerging as potential tools to address these limitations. We conducted a scoping review with narrative synthesis of literature on human factors, ergonomics, AI, robotic technologies, and shared autonomy in colonoscopy and surgical robotics. Evidence synthesis: Colonoscopy performance remains limited by non-negligible miss rates and variability driven by both technical and human factors. Ergonomic constraints and cognitive workload contribute significantly to operator strain and may affect vigilance and decision-making. AI systems-including computer-aided detection (CADe), diagnosis (CADx), and quality monitoring-have demonstrated improvements in detection metrics and procedural standardisation, although concerns regarding cognitive offloading and potential deskilling persist. In parallel, emerging robotic and soft-robotic platforms aim to enhance navigation, improve procedural ergonomics, and reduce operator musculoskeletal strain, although clinical evidence remains limited. These technologies converge within a task-based shared-autonomy paradigm integrating physical, perceptual, and cognitive augmentation, with different procedural tasks operating at different levels of human-system control. A task-based shared-autonomy framework may provide a coherent model for integrating AI and robotics into colonoscopy while preserving human supervision and clinical judgement. Future developments should prioritise human-centred design, workflow integration, and multidimensional evaluation strategies to ensure safe and effective clinical implementation.

items.title: Autonomous Robotic Systems in Agriculture 5.0: A Review on Technical Architecture, Operational Applications, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: This comprehensive narrative review examines the current state and future development perspectives of autonomous robotic systems within the scope of the Agriculture 5.0 paradigm, which aims for sustainable and efficient agricultural production. In this paper, the cognitive and physical structure of robotic systems is addressed through the "Eye-Brain-Foot Hand" hierarchy, and the role of next-generation Vision-Language Action (VLA) models, such as RT-2 and OpenVLA, in contextual agronomic decision-making processes is analyzed. Within the scope of field applications, the SAM2-based SPAF framework, which offers 95.54% harvesting success rate in tomatoes, and spot-spraying technologies that reduce chemical input volume by 90% are evaluated using quantitative data. Furthermore, the synergy between heterogeneous UAV-UGV fleets, trust-building through Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), and emerging advanced technological approaches such as Quantum Reinforcement Learning (QRL) are assessed. The results demonstrate that autonomous agriculture is not merely a tool to enhance technical efficiency, but is transforming into a cyber-physical production ecosystem where ethical responsibility, data sovereignty, and environmental sustainability converge.
